title: What We Learned Deploying AI within Bloomberg’s Engineering Organization – Lei Zhang, Bloomberg
talk_summary: Bloomberg's infrastructure lead describes deploying AI coding tools across 9,000 engineers, focusing on 'golden path' enablement: a model gateway, an MCP directory, a standard deployment pipeline, and uplift/incident-response agents. Key lessons are that AI increases open PRs and time-to-merge, that deterministic verification is the bottleneck, and that adoption spreads through onboarding and communities rather than mandates.

takeaways.technique: Treat review/merge capacity as the binding constraint, not code generation
takeaways.what_they_do: They observed that generating patches with AI increased average open PRs and time-to-merge because humans still had to review and merge the new code, so they frame review throughput as the real bottleneck to solve.
takeaways.evidence_quote: the average open pull requests increased and time to merge also increased uh because you spin a lot of new code and then still we have to review the code and merge the code

takeaways.technique: Deterministic verification as the gate for AI patches
takeaways.what_they_do: They say AI/ML patches need deterministic verification (tests, linters) to be reliably applicable; without good verification the patch quality is hard to trust, which is why their uplift agents beat regex refactoring only when verification exists.
takeaways.evidence_quote: it would be really nice if there's some detistic verification capability ... if you don't have good llinter if you don't have good verification the the patch can sometimes be uh uh difficult to to to be applied

takeaways.technique: Central model gateway with visibility and guided model choice
takeaways.what_they_do: A single gateway lets teams experiment with models, gives central visibility into which models are used, and lets the platform team recommend the best-fit model per problem.
takeaways.evidence_quote: we have a gateway so that teams can easily figure out which model works the best. They can do quick experiments. they can um we can have visibility what kind of models being used

takeaways.technique: MCP/tool directory to prevent duplicate agent tooling
takeaways.what_they_do: Before teams build MCP servers, they publish a discovery hub so teams find existing servers and partner instead of duplicating; tool creation/deployment goes through a standard platform pipeline with runtime handled for them.
takeaways.evidence_quote: we have a two discovery uh basically MCP directory via hub so that let's say team A wants to do something they will go to the hub okay someone is building MCB server already maybe I should partner with them

takeaways.technique: Point agents at low-preference maintenance work (uplift/migrations)
takeaways.what_they_do: Rather than only greenfield coding, they target work developers dislike (maintenance, migrations) with 'uplift agents' that scan the codebase, find applicable patches, and attach the fix plus rationale to the ticket.
takeaways.evidence_quote: maybe we can also look into some of the work our developers don't really prefer to do for instance um some men work some of the migration work

takeaways.technique: Onboarding + community as the adoption/quality lever
takeaways.what_they_do: They embed AI coding into existing onboarding so new hires learn the sanctioned way and then push back on senior staff, and they bootstrap a cross-org community to share learnings and reduce duplicated effort.
takeaways.evidence_quote: whenever we have folks join a company they learn how to do things in new way when they go back to their team they were like hey why don't we do that
